items.title: The missing middle in India's growth story
items.syllabus: GS3 › Growth, development and employment; Inclusive growth; Infrastructure; Energy · GS1 › Effects of globalisation; Social stratification
items.summary: India has stayed lower-middle income for 19 years while Vietnam and China moved up fast; five statistics show jobs, factories, private investment, power and a thin middle class holding it back.
evolution: India enters the World Bank's lower-middle-income group.
Vietnam, lower-middle income since 2009, moves up to upper-middle income this year: about 16 years.
China moves from lower-middle to upper-middle income in 13 years.
India still lower-middle income, 19 years on; five countries move up this year.
ideas: Stuck in the middle: India has been lower-middle income for 19 years; Vietnam and China moved up in 16 and 13. At 8.5% dollar growth, against 5.4% in the past decade, India could get there in about six years.
GS3 · Growth / middle-income trap
Nineteen years after turning lower-middle income, India is still there, while Vietnam took 16 years and China 13 to move up.

Jobs without productivity: the labour force grew by 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women, mostly self-employed in farming; 43% still work in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal firms.
GS3 employment · GS1 women
Employment is not productive employment: 43% of India's workers remain in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers in informal enterprises.

Factories but no factory jobs: registered factories doubled, yet manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen; more workers joined the gig economy than formal manufacturing, and capital-intensive growth widened inequality.
GS3 · Manufacturing / inequality
Though registered factories doubled to 2.6 lakh, manufacturing has not become India's ladder of mass upward mobility.
Public investment has not crowded in private investment: infrastructure cut logistics costs, but firms repaired balance sheets and rewarded shareholders instead of investing.
GS3 · Investment
Public infrastructure spending was meant to crowd in private investment, but the private sector has not taken the baton.
Power is a binding constraint: solar has outrun storage and transmission, so output was curtailed even as demand peaked, hurting factories, data centres and AI.
GS3 · Energy / infrastructure
Solar generation running ahead of storage and transmission makes electricity a constraint on India's manufacturing and AI ambitions.
Rich faster than a middle class: 9.4 lakh dollar millionaires, but a broad middle class is not forming; premiumisation and capital outflows follow.
GS3 inclusive growth · GS1 inequality
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class, the missing middle of its growth story.
keywords: Countries stuck at middle income, unable to move up
Without productive jobs, India risks a middle-income trap.
Workers moving from farms to factories and modern services
India's structural transformation has stalled: workers left farms for informal work, not factories.
Jobs with rising output and income per worker
Being employed is not the same as being productively employed.
Work that adds little output, taken because unemployment is unaffordable
The poor cannot afford to be unemployed, so low unemployment hides underemployment.
Public investment drawing in private investment
Public capex has not crowded in private investment.
Growth driven by machines more than labour
Capital-intensive manufacturing has raised profits faster than wages.
Premiumisation reflects growth concentrated at the top.
Women forming a growing share of farm work
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in farming.
data: Rise in India's labour force in less than a decade; two-thirds women
India's labour force grew by over 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women (World Bank).
Workforce still in agriculture / non-farm workers in informal enterprises
43% of India's workers are in agriculture, and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal enterprises.
Registered factories doubled from 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh, yet manufacturing's share stayed flat.
examples: Vietnam
Lower-middle income in 2009; moved up to upper-middle income this year, about 16 years later
Best practice: export-led manufacturing
Vietnam moved from lower- to upper-middle income in 16 years, a model of manufacturing-led growth.
China
Upper-middle income in 2010, 13 years after becoming lower-middle
Best practice: factory-led mobility
China reached upper-middle income in just 13 years by putting workers on factory floors.
Solar curtailment, summer 2026
Solar output cut despite peak demand, for lack of storage and transmission
Energy constraint
In summer 2026, India curtailed solar power even at peak demand for lack of storage and grid.
pyqs: India skipped the manufacturing stage; the missing middle is the result.
Jobs grew with the labour force, but not productive jobs.
Manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive: factories doubled, factory jobs did not.
Industrial growth lagging GDP: manufacturing's share has not risen.
Growth led by more labour, not productivity: the 100 million new workers are mostly in low-value work.
Manufacturing's share in GDP and MSMEs: the core of the missing middle.
Infrastructure investment has cut logistics costs but not yet crowded in private investment.

trend.t: UPSC has asked the same structural question for a decade: India moved from agriculture to services and skipped manufacturing (2014), growth has been jobless (2015), manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive (2017) and growth rests on more labour, not productivity (2022). The latest questions ask for solutions: manufacturing and MSMEs (2023) and labour codes (2024).
trend.watch: Manufacturing and productive employment have come in 2014, 2017 (twice), 2022 and 2023. Structural transformation is a must-study area in GS3.
focus: Manufacturing-led jobs: PLI, MSMEs, labour-intensive sectors
Crowding in private investment after public capex
Power, storage and transmission as constraints on industry
Inequality and the middle class; women's productive employment

potential: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale. (15 marks)
Why has manufacturing not become the engine of employment in India despite the rise in registered factories? Examine. (10 marks)
Public investment in infrastructure has not crowded in private investment. Analyse the reasons and suggest measures. (10 marks)
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class. Examine the implications for inclusive growth. (10 marks)

practice.q: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale.
parts: Introduction: India's 19 years at lower-middle income vs Vietnam and China (one line, with facts)
Strategy for high-productivity jobs (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has been lower-middle income since 2007, while Vietnam moved up in 16 years and China in 13 (World Bank).

pts.t: Workers moved from farms into informal work, not factories.
pts.ex: 43% still in agriculture; 79% of non-farm workers informal.

pts.t: Factories doubled, but manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen.
pts.ex: 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh registered factories, 2004-05 to 2024-25.

pts.t: Machines over labour keep wages behind profits and raise inequality.
Firms deleveraged and paid shareholders instead of building capacity, despite public capex.
Solar outruns storage and transmission, so supply is unreliable.
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in agriculture.
Many workers lack skills for modern manufacturing and services.
Wealth concentrates at the top, limiting broad-based demand.
Prioritise textiles, apparel, footwear, electronics assembly and food processing.
Tie incentives to employment, not just output.
Credit, technology and easier compliance.
Predictable policy, faster clearances and demand certainty.
Storage, transmission and reliable, affordable supply.
Vocational training, childcare and safe transport to bring women into factories.
Flexibility for firms with social security for workers.

answer.t: India can escape the middle-income trap only by moving its workers from low- to high-productivity jobs, with public infrastructure and private capital working together.

items.title: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills, literacy
items.where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Tim Curtis, UNESCO)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Internal security: role of media and social networking sites; Cyber security; Science and technology: AI · GS2 › Important international institutions (UNESCO); Education (digital and media literacy); Elections · GS4 › Ethics in media and technology; Role of education in inculcating values
items.summary: UNESCO's South Asia head argues that laws and AI labels cannot keep pace with AI-made misinformation; India must build media and information literacy (MIL) for all, with platforms, newsrooms and creators sharing the job.
ideas: From access to judgement: generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap, so the question is no longer how to find information but how to judge what is reliable. Media and information literacy (MIL) is the answer.
GS3 · AI and misinformation
With generative AI making fakes cheap, the challenge has shifted from accessing information to judging it, which makes media and information literacy essential.
Connectivity is not capability: India has over a billion internet subscribers, but few can navigate the information space; platforms reward emotionally charged content, which deepens polarisation.
GS3 · Digital divide / social media
India's billion internet users show connectivity, not capability: only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online.
Misinformation does most harm in crises and elections, when people most need reliable information.
GS3 internal security · GS2 elections
Misinformation is most dangerous in crises and elections, as out-of-context flood videos in Nepal and a fake AI audio in Slovakia's election show.

Laws and labels are not enough: labelling AI content helps, but no law or detection tool can match the speed of synthetic content; people need skills, through trained teachers, local-language materials, and outreach beyond classrooms to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
GS3 · Way forward / GS2 education
No law or detection tool can keep pace with AI fakes; lasting defence lies in citizens' skills, taught in local languages and beyond classrooms.

'We All Play a Part': platforms must be transparent about algorithms, label synthetic media and moderate beyond English and Hindi; newsrooms must explain how they verify; creators need verification skills and ethics.
GS3 governance · GS4 media ethics
Countering misinformation is a shared duty: transparent platforms, newsrooms that explain verification, and creators trained in ethics.
MIL is an investment in democracy: children grow up in AI-shaped feeds before they can question them, so MIL builds critical thinking, social trust and collective resilience.
GS2 democracy · Essay
Media literacy is not just safe technology use; it is an investment in critical thinking, social trust and democratic resilience.
keywords: Ability to access, understand, evaluate and share information responsibly
Media and information literacy is the most durable defence against AI-made misinformation.
AI that creates realistic text, images, audio and video
Generative AI has made synthetic media cheap and convincing.
AI-made fake audio or video of real people
A deepfake audio before Slovakia's 2023 election shows the threat to elections.
Labelling AI content helps but cannot stop deception or the misuse of genuine footage.
Platforms promoting content that grabs attention, often emotional
Platforms built for attention amplify emotionally charged and divisive content.
Content moderation beyond English and Hindi
Policing harmful content in all Indian languages
In multilingual India, moderation must work beyond English and Hindi.
Real evidence dismissed as fake because fakes are common
The spread of deepfakes lets people dismiss genuine footage as fake: the liar's dividend.
A society's shared ability to resist manipulation
MIL builds collective resilience against disinformation.
data: Digital India / scale of the challenge
India has over a billion internet subscribers (TRAI).
People aged 15+ able to file a cybercrime complaint through the official portal
Only 18% of Indians aged 15 and above can file a cybercrime complaint online (NSO, 2025).
examples: UNESCO Global Media and Information Literacy Week (2026)
Theme: 'We All Play a Part: Media and Information Literacy for the People'
Global initiative / shared responsibility
UNESCO's 2026 MIL Week theme, 'We All Play a Part', stresses that countering misinformation is everyone's job.
Nepal floods, August 2026
Videos with images taken out of context circulated online
Misinformation in disasters
During Nepal's August floods, out-of-context videos distorted public understanding when reliable information mattered most.
UNESCO Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms
A framework for platform transparency and accountability
Best practice in platform governance
UNESCO's Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms offer a framework for transparency and accountability.
Slovakia's 2023 election
An AI-generated audio falsely implicated politicians two days before the vote
AI and elections
An AI-faked audio two days before Slovakia's 2023 election shows the risk to electoral integrity.
UNESCO's 'AI Answers. You Decide' module
Teaches learners how AI works and how to assess its outputs
Best practice in AI literacy
UNESCO's 'AI Answers. You Decide' module teaches students to question AI outputs.
pyqs: Directly usable: fake news threatens internal security; MIL complements the amended IT Rules.
Social media as a security challenge: AI-made misinformation is the newest form.
Misuse of social media: today the tool is generative AI, the answer includes literacy.
AI's risks include cheap, fast misinformation.
Disaster resilience includes reliable information; misinformation during Nepal's floods shows the risk.
Ethical issues of social media: platform, creator and user responsibility.
Relying on AI outputs without judgement is an ethical risk; MIL teaches people to question them.

trend.t: Social media has moved through the papers from a tool of terror (ISIS recruitment 2015, non-state actors 2016) to a security challenge (social media and encryption 2024) to fake news and its regulation (IT Rules 2026). GS4 has added the ethics of social media (2025) and of AI (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Social media and misinformation have come in four GS3 papers and in GS4 2025, and AI in 2023, 2024 and 2026. AI-driven misinformation joins both threads and is a must-study topic.
focus: Deepfakes and AI misinformation in elections and public order
Media and information literacy as a long-term solution
Platform governance: IT Rules, labelling AI content, transparency of algorithms

potential: Generative AI has made misinformation cheaper and faster. Discuss the threats it poses to democracy and internal security in India and suggest a strategy that goes beyond regulation. (15 marks)
'Connectivity does not automatically translate into capability.' Examine the need for media and information literacy in India. (10 marks)
Discuss the role of digital platforms in countering misinformation. Should they be regulated more strictly? (10 marks)

practice.q: Generative AI has made misinformation cheaper and faster. Discuss the threats it poses to democracy and internal security in India and suggest a strategy that goes beyond regulation.
parts: Introduction: generative AI and the misinformation challenge (one line, with facts)
Threats to democracy and internal security
Strategy beyond regulation (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has over a billion internet users (TRAI), yet only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online (NSO, 2025), and generative AI now makes convincing fakes cheap.

answer.h: Threats to democracy and internal security

pts.t: Deepfakes released just before polls can sway voters before they are debunked.
pts.ex: AI audio two days before Slovakia's 2023 election.

pts.t: Fabricated videos can spark violence within hours.
False content in crises misleads people when they most need facts.
Algorithms reward outrage, splitting society into hostile camps.
When fakes abound, genuine evidence is also doubted (the liar's dividend).
AI voice clones and fake identities enable scams.
Synthetic content spreads faster than any law or detection tool can act.
Labelling AI content cannot stop deception or the misuse of genuine footage.
Heavy regulation risks censorship of legitimate expression.
Moderation rarely works well beyond English and Hindi.
Content and platforms often lie outside Indian jurisdiction.
Many users cannot report or verify content.
pts.ex: Only 18% can file a cybercrime complaint online.

pts.k: Media and information literacy in schools
pts.t: Teach students to evaluate sources, spot bias and understand algorithms, with trained teachers and local-language material.
Bring MIL to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
Community radio, local journalists and health workers can share verified information, especially in emergencies.
Transparent algorithms, labelled synthetic media and rapid crisis response.
pts.ex: UNESCO Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms.

pts.t: Explain verification; train influencers in fact-checking and ethics.
Government, platforms, media, schools and citizens each play a part.
pts.ex: UNESCO MIL Week 2026: 'We All Play a Part'.

answer.t: Laws can slow misinformation, but only a media-literate public can defeat it; MIL is an investment in democracy itself.

items.title: Inter-State Council is a meeting point that has withered away. It must be rebuilt
items.syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; Issues and challenges pertaining to the federal structure; Centre-State relations; Constitutional bodies
items.summary: Shashi Tharoor argues that decisions like delimitation need the states' voice, and the Inter-State Council under Article 263, dormant for years, must be revived as an autonomous forum for Centre-state consultation.
evolution: Article 263 empowers the President to set up a council for Centre-state coordination.
Sarkaria Commission calls the dormant Inter-State Council the 'missing link'; the Council is constituted in 1990.
Long gaps between meetings; the Council works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Debate over a delimitation bill; Tharoor calls for reviving the Council before such decisions.
ideas: States must be heard on delimitation: deciding it in Parliament alone bypasses the states, an essential part of the federal system.
GS2 · Federalism / delimitation
A change as basic as delimitation should follow a national conversation that includes the states, not Parliament alone.
Article 263 envisioned a meeting point: the founders created the Inter-State Council to balance a strongly centralised Constitution in a diverse country.
GS2 · Constitutional bodies
Article 263 was meant to temper India's centralising Constitution with a forum for Centre-state coordination.
The 'missing link': the Council lay dormant for four decades and was set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice.
GS2 · Centre-state relations
The Sarkaria Commission called the dormant Inter-State Council the missing link in India's federal equilibrium.
Withered by design: without operational autonomy or regular meetings, it became an appendage of the Home Ministry, preferring unilateral policymaking over dialogue.
GS2 · Institutional weakness
Without operational autonomy or regular meetings, the Inter-State Council has become a minor arm of the Home Ministry.
Its atrophy erodes trust, especially with opposition-ruled states, as policy on tax, health, environment and security cuts across jurisdictions.
GS2 · Cooperative vs confrontational federalism
When the Inter-State Council is dormant, top-down policy breeds friction, especially with opposition-ruled states.
Rebuild it: an independent statutory secretariat, fixed meetings of the PM and CMs, and a role in major reforms, scheme reviews and inter-state disputes, giving 'cooperative federalism' a platform.
GS2 · Way forward
A revived Inter-State Council would give 'cooperative federalism' a platform, not just a slogan.
keywords: Constitutional basis for the Inter-State Council
Article 263 empowers the President to set up an Inter-State Council for Centre-state coordination.
Led to the Inter-State Council's creation in 1990
On the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation, the Inter-State Council was set up in 1990.
Freedom to set its agenda and function independently
The Council lacks the operational autonomy to act as a genuine federal forum.
Sarkaria's description of the dormant Inter-State Council
The Inter-State Council remains the missing link in India's federal equilibrium.
Centre and states working together as partners
Cooperative federalism has remained 'a platitude without a platform'.
Gradual weakening of an institution through neglect
Institutional atrophy has left a void at the heart of Indian federalism.
Redrawing seats and their distribution among states
Delimitation without the states' voice risks a federal crisis.
Mutual suspicion between the Centre and states
The Council's atrophy has deepened the Centre-state trust deficit.
examples: Inter-State Council (1990)
Set up on the Sarkaria Commission's advice, but met rarely and became a Home Ministry appendage
Weak federal institution
The Inter-State Council, set up in 1990, has met only at long intervals.
Delimitation debate (2026)
A bill feared to tilt seats towards some states, with no forum for states' views
Need for consultation
The 2026 delimitation debate shows why states need a formal forum.
pyqs: Directly usable: drawbacks of cooperative federalism; a dormant Inter-State Council is one.
Cooperation, competition, confrontation: a dormant Council tilts the balance to confrontation.
Recent changes in Centre-state relations; measures to build trust include reviving the Inter-State Council.
Dispute-resolution mechanisms in the federal framework: the Inter-State Council is the constitutional one.
Regional parties seek autonomy; a forum for states' views eases the tension.
Federalism as a basic feature is weakened when states are not consulted.

trend.t: Federalism has been asked almost every year: cooperative federalism (2015), cooperation versus confrontation (2020), national versus regional parties (2022), recent changes in Centre-state relations (2024), fiscal relations (2025) and dispute-resolution mechanisms (2026), alongside the Governor (2022, 2026) and Article 356 (2023). The focus has moved from the nature of Indian federalism to the institutions that should make it work.
trend.watch: Centre-state relations come up in nearly every GS2 paper. Institutional mechanisms (Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, GST Council, Finance Commission) and delimitation are must-study.
focus: Reviving the Inter-State Council and other Centre-state forums
Delimitation and the balance between states
The Governor's role and Centre-state friction
Fiscal federalism: GST, Finance Commission, state finances

potential: The Inter-State Council has remained a 'missing link' in India's federal structure. Examine the reasons for its ineffectiveness and suggest measures to make it a genuine platform for cooperative federalism. (15 marks)
Should delimitation of constituencies be preceded by consultation with the states? Discuss in the context of Indian federalism. (10 marks)
'Cooperative federalism has remained a platitude without a platform.' Critically examine. (10 marks)

practice.q: The Inter-State Council has remained a 'missing link' in India's federal structure. Examine the reasons for its ineffectiveness and suggest measures to make it a genuine platform for cooperative federalism.
parts: Introduction: Article 263, Sarkaria, 1990 (one line, with facts)

answer.t: Envisaged under Article 263 and set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice, the Inter-State Council has met rarely, leaving Centre-state dialogue without a forum.

pts.t: A forum where states shape national policy in a diverse country.
Tax, health, environment and security cut across jurisdictions.
Delimitation and resource sharing need states' consent.
A neutral platform for Centre-state and inter-state disputes.
Regular dialogue reduces friction and litigation.
States can assess the local impact of central schemes.
It works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Years pass between meetings despite the obligation to meet.
Its recommendations do not bind the Centre.
Governments favour central decisions or informal deals.
Opposition-ruled states see it as a Centre-controlled forum.
NITI Aayog and other bodies dilute its role.
Convene the PM, key ministers and CMs at regular intervals.
A statutory secretariat with civil servants and experts.
Require consultation on delimitation, major reforms and state-specific laws.
Use it for inter-state disputes on water, resources and infrastructure.
A working model of shared decision-making.
No new law is needed; Article 263 already allows it.

answer.t: Reviving the Inter-State Council would give cooperative federalism a platform, turning Centre-state relations from confrontation into partnership.

items.title: RBI to hire agency to manage social media presence
items.syllabus: GS2 › E-governance; Transparency and accountability · GS3 › Monetary policy and its communication · GS4 › Citizen-centric governance; Quality of service delivery
items.summary: The RBI has invited bids for an agency to run its social media round the clock, with podcasts, digital content and responses to the public, to communicate better in a digital-first information environment.
ideas: E-governance: the RBI is taking its policies, decisions and public-awareness messages directly to citizens through social media and podcasts.
GS2 · E-governance
The RBI's round-the-clock social media outreach shows public institutions adapting to a digital-first information environment.
Clear communication strengthens monetary policy: when people understand the central bank's signals, policy works better.
GS3 · Monetary policy
Effective communication by the RBI makes monetary policy more credible and effective.
People-centric good governance: listening to online conversations and answering the public makes an institution more transparent and responsive.
GS4 · Citizen-centric governance
By tracking and answering public responses online, the RBI models citizen-centric, responsive governance.
keywords: A setting where people get information mainly online
Public institutions must communicate effectively in a digital-first information environment.
Governance designed around citizens' needs and feedback
Two-way digital outreach makes governance citizen-centric.
How the RBI explains its policy to markets and the public
Clear central bank communication anchors public expectations.
examples: RBI's social media tender (Oct 2026)
24x7 social media, podcasts, digital content and public responses, run by its Department of Communication
GS4
Best practice: people-centric, good governance
The RBI's 2026 move to run 24x7 social media and podcasts is a best practice in people-centric governance.
pyqs: Good governance and e-governance: the RBI's direct digital outreach to citizens is an example.

items.title: Noel Tata to step down from six Tata company boards at 70
items.syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: corporate governance · GS4 › Corporate governance; Good governance
items.summary: Noel Tata, Chairman of Tata Trusts, will leave the boards of six Tata companies on 12 November when he turns 70, following the group's retirement policy for non-executive directors; he stays at Tata Trusts.
ideas: Rule-based corporate governance: a fixed retirement age for non-executive directors applies equally, even to the top family name.
GS3 · Corporate governance
Uniform, rule-based board policies, like Tata's retirement age for non-executive directors, strengthen corporate governance.
Good governance in practice: following one's own rules builds trust among shareholders and the public.
GS4 · Good governance
When leaders follow the rules they set, institutions gain credibility and public trust.
keywords: Decisions guided by clear, uniform rules, not individuals
Rule-based governance limits personal discretion and builds trust.
Planned exit of directors to bring in fresh leadership
Retirement policies enable regular board renewal.
examples: Noel Tata's board exit (Nov 2026)
Steps down from Trent, Voltas, Tata Investment Corp, Tata International, Tata Steel and Titan at 70
GS4
Best practice: good governance in the corporate sector
Noel Tata stepping down at 70 under the group's retirement policy shows rules applying equally to all.
pyqs: Corporate governance reforms: rule-based board policies are an example.

essay.use: For 'There can be no social justice without economic prosperity but economic prosperity without social justice is meaningless' (2020).
